definition: Avenge means to get revenge for a wrong done to oneself or another.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word avenge. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know avenge should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The colony's lone survivor spends the sequel avenging her crew, hunting the saboteur across three star systems.
Complaining answers a wrong with words only — far weaker than avenging it.
Retaliate strikes back in kind, tit for tat, but it stops short of avenge, which claims full justice for a serious wrong.

Requite is the formal, slightly old-fashioned word for repaying treatment in kind — and the treatment can be good or ill: devotion can be requited, and so can an insult. Avenge answers only wrongs, and serious ones; nobody avenges a favor. Requite balances any ledger; avenge settles a grievance.

To punish is to impose a penalty from a position of authority — impersonal, lawful, owed to no one's grief. To avenge is personal: you avenge a wrong done to yourself or to someone you care for, claiming justice with your own hands. The law punishes; the wronged avenge.

Every verse of the old ballad circles back to vengeance.
Avenge means to get revenge for a wrong done to oneself or another.
The deposed duchess waited twenty years to avenge her exile, returning at the head of an army of the very miners her rival had starved.
Avenge is not simple payback: it answers a real wrong, often on someone else's behalf, and claims justice while it does.
You retaliate for a shove; you avenge a betrayal, a ruin, a death — the word asks the wrong to be worthy of it.
Avenge claims justice for a real wrong, often on another's behalf — a queen avenges her father; you merely get even over a parking spot.
For tit-for-tat answers, retaliate is the honest word; avenge dignifies the payback, so spend it only where the wrong has weight.

When Ruth Calloway lost her savings to a phony investment club in 1987, the police file stayed thin and the money stayed gone.
Her grandson Marcus, nine at the time, is candid about what drove the next twenty years: he wanted to avenge her.
He became a fraud investigator.
He learned the con's every variation.
And in 2009 he traced its inventor -- still running the same scheme -- and handed prosecutors a case they could not drop.
'The state punished him,' Marcus says.
'That part was never mine to do.
Mine was making sure it happened for her.' Ruth died in 2011, eighteen months after watching the verdict read aloud, her hand in her grandson's.
